title:
Getting started on the
Illinois Campus Cluster
body: A practical workflow for data analysis
notes: We will follow a project from requesting access to reading a completed job’s output. The same HPC routine supports bulk, single-cell, and spatial analysis: prepare files, make the software available, request resources, run the script, and check its results. This lecture explains that routine from the beginning. The small files and job outputs shown here are teaching examples, not research results.

title: Prepare files on login nodes; run jobs on compute nodes
notes:
HPC means high-performance computing. Follow the official figure from the researcher’s laptop to the head node, also called a login node. The job arrow leads to the compute nodes. Shared storage lets both stages reach the project files. A node is one computer.

Walkthrough: point to the laptop, login/head node, job arrow, compute nodes, and storage in that order. The detailed labels are references; focus the explanation on connect, submit, and read the result. Opening VS Code does not itself allocate a compute node. Use the login connection for file work and short lightweight checks, and scheduled resources for substantial analysis.

title: Request access and confirm your allocation details
body:
Existing lab accessAsk the PI or technical contact which investor group to join.
A new computing needStart an Illinois Computes request.
Keep this detailUsed for
NetIDYour login identity
Slurm accountThe group’s compute allocation
PartitionA queue you may submit to
Project pathAn approved writable folder
Research access request ↗Illinois Computes request ↗

Wait for approval and confirm these details and Duo access before connecting.
notes:
Begin with the group’s PI or technical contact. A member of an existing investor group follows that access route. A new need can start with Illinois Computes. A form begins the request; login requires completed approval and provisioning. Prepare a brief description of the software and data size.

NetID identifies you. The Slurm account identifies the allocation, and the partition identifies the queue. Keep the valid account and partition together. The project path is a separate file location. If account details are missing after approval, ICC provides /sw/cc.users/tools/my.accounts on a login node. Ask the group to confirm the matching queue. This lecture does not choose an allocation for the viewer.

title: The first SSH login
body:
On your laptop: open Terminal (macOS) or PowerShell (Windows)
ssh YOUR_NETID@cc-login.campuscluster.illinois.edu

ssh starts the connection · before @: your user name · after @: the cluster address

1 · Run the commandReplace YOUR_NETID, then press Enter.
2 · PasswordType your NetID password and press Enter; typing stays hidden.
3 · DuoFollow the prompt and approve the authentication request.
notes:
On macOS, open Terminal from Spotlight; on Windows, search for PowerShell or Windows Terminal. The SSH client runs on the laptop. Type the command there, substituting the actual NetID without adding angle brackets. The at sign separates the user name from the host address. Press Enter to send the command. If ssh is not found on Windows, enable the OpenSSH Client optional feature or follow the institution’s setup guidance.

The first connection may ask whether the host is authentic. Verify the host fingerprint through institutional guidance or support before accepting; do not treat an unexpected changed-host warning as routine. Type the NetID password even though characters are not shown, then follow the Duo prompt. If 1 is offered for a push notification, select it and approve on the registered device. ICC requires password plus Duo and does not permit user-generated SSH keys.

The welcome message and a prompt on cc-login indicate a remote shell. Commands typed there now execute on the cluster. The screenshot’s quota values and dates are historical examples. The next step uses VS Code, which opens its own SSH session; it does not require keeping this initial terminal test open. At the remote prompt, exit closes this test connection without deleting files.

title: VS Code is an editor for code and project files
body:
Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is Microsoft’s code editor for working with scripts and project files.

B · ExplorerBrowse files and folders in the left sidebar.
C · EditorRead and edit scripts in the main area.
D · TerminalEnter commands in the bottom panel.
notes:
Introduce the full name, Visual Studio Code, before using the abbreviation VS Code. It is a desktop application that puts file browsing, editing, and a terminal in one window. The screenshot is an official Microsoft example, not an ICC session. Its code and file names are not commands to copy.

Point to B on the left: this sidebar currently shows the Explorer and its file tree. Point to C: the open editor areas show file contents. Point to D: the bottom panel currently contains the terminal, where commands can be entered. The panel can also show other views. These are the three areas we will use; the other labels can wait.

Next, we will connect this editor to files on the cluster. The following diagram explains how the local VS Code window reaches the remote project.

title: Use local VS Code to edit files on the cluster
body:
On your laptopThe VS Code window and its controls
On the clusterThe project files and remote terminal processes

Remote editing gives you a familiar interface to the files on the cluster.
notes:
Use Microsoft’s diagram to explain where things live. The editor window is local. The SSH connection reaches the remote environment and project files. The diagram includes extension and debugging details, but they are not needed for the first workflow.

Walkthrough: point to the local VS Code box, the connection, and the source-code box on the right. Explain that a save writes to the remote file. Resource allocation is a separate step handled by Slurm; the diagram does not mean every program started from the editor already has a compute allocation.

title: Files stay on the cluster; terminal commands run there
body:
LOCAL Your laptop
VS Code window
View and editanalysis.pyYour screen, keyboard, and mouse
Remote - SSH
⟷
View · edit · save
REMOTE The cluster
Project filesdemo/analysis.pySave updates this file.
Remote terminalCommands run on the cluster.

In the SSH window, you work with files and a terminal on the cluster.
notes:
Read the diagram from left to right. The VS Code application and the visible window are on the laptop. Remote - SSH connects that window to a remote project and remote terminal. The file named analysis.py is shown in the editor, but saving writes to demo/analysis.py on the cluster. This figure shows the state after the small project has been uploaded; the next slides explain how to connect and upload it.

Point to the remote terminal on the right. Although its text appears in the laptop window, its commands run on the connected cluster host. In this course that connection initially reaches a login node. An ordinary local terminal would run commands on the laptop. SSH opens a connection; Slurm will allocate compute resources later. The diagram is a simplified teaching schematic, not a live VS Code screenshot.

This distinction explains the practical benefit: edit and save the remote file directly, then use the remote terminal when a command is needed. Next install the local editor and its connection extension.

title: Install VS Code and the Remote - SSH extension
body:
Install VS CodeDownload the desktop application for your operating system.
Open ExtensionsClick the Extensions icon in VS Code’s left sidebar.
SearchEnter Remote - SSH; choose the extension published by Microsoft.
InstallClick Install and wait until it finishes.
Official VS Code setup ↗

This installs the editor and connection tool on your laptop.
notes:
VS Code is the local graphical application used throughout the lecture. Install and launch it before trying to connect. In Extensions, identify Microsoft as the publisher of Remote - SSH and click Install. These are local setup actions, performed once. Installing this extension does not install Python or analysis packages on the cluster.

After the extension is ready, the Command Palette will contain Remote-SSH connection actions. The next slide uses the same NetID and hostname that worked in the terminal. A new remote VS Code window may open.

title: Connecting VS Code with Remote - SSH
body:
Command PaletteCmd+Shift+P on macOS; Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows/Linux
ChooseRemote-SSH: Connect to Host…
Enter and sign inYOUR_NETID@cc-login.campuscluster.illinois.edu

Complete password + Duo. Choose Linux if asked. The lower-left indicator should show SSH and the host.
notes:
Use the local VS Code application with Microsoft’s Remote - SSH extension. The Command Palette starts the connection. Enter the same user and host used for SSH, then authenticate. ICC is a Linux remote system.

Walkthrough: show the extension name and publisher, the Command Palette, the host entry, and finally the SSH indicator. If authentication is waiting out of sight, inspect the Remote - SSH output or login terminal. The essential benefit is remote file access in a familiar editor.

title: Choose home, project, or scratch storage
body:
LocationUse it forRemember
/u/YOUR_NETIDSettings and small personal filesVery limited quota: 100 GiB (soft limit). Keep large datasets elsewhere.
/projects/YOUR_GROUPGroup data, software, and retained outputsShared group quota; no snapshots. Keep a separate backup of important files.
/scratch/YOUR_NETIDTemporary working dataTemporary only: files typically deleted after 30 days without access, sometimes sooner.

For this example: /projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
notes:
Before uploading, identify the authorized writable location supplied by the group. Throughout the worked example, /projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo stands for that project folder. It is a placeholder, not a directory that every user can access. Replace the group path with the actual approved path.

Quota means your storage allowance. ICC lists home at 100 GiB soft / 103 GiB hard; the quota cannot be expanded. Over the soft limit for seven days, new writes stop until usage is reduced. Project capacity is shared and depends on the group’s allocation; no snapshots are provided. Keep separate backups. Scratch cleanup typically uses 30 days since last access, but can happen sooner when space runs low. Purged files are unrecoverable. Move important outputs out of scratch. Policies checked on 28 October 2026. We will put the input, scripts, environment, and final result in the same durable project directory. Now open its parent location in VS Code.

title: Open the remote project location
body:
File → Open FolderOpen /projects/YOUR_GROUP or your assigned path.
Check the connectionThe SSH indicator should identify the cluster.
Find the destinationThis is where the demo folder will be uploaded.

The Explorer now shows the remote location, before the upload.
notes:
Use the Open Folder dialog shown in Microsoft’s screenshot. Its personal sample path is not an ICC path to copy. Open the authorized parent directory obtained during account setup. Check the SSH indicator to confirm that Explorer is showing the remote filesystem.

At this point the demo folder still lives on the laptop. We have chosen the destination but have not transferred the project. The next slide performs that transfer. This separation makes it clear which folder is local and which is on the cluster.

title: Upload the demo folder with VS Code
body:
On the laptopUnzip the offline package; find HPC_Introduction/demo.
UploadDrag demo into the remote Explorer destination.
Open the projectFile → Open Folder → /projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
Check a fileOpen data/samples.csv and look for the three sample rows.

Wait for the transfer to finish. The input and scripts now live on the cluster.
notes:
First unzip HPC_Introduction_Offline.zip on the laptop. Inside the extracted HPC_Introduction folder, find demo. Its input and scripts are already supplied; listeners do not need to write or invent them. The offline package includes a small demo folder containing only the files for the main Python route. Drag that folder into the remote Explorer directory, not onto an editor tab. When the upload is complete, use Open Folder again to select the new demo directory. Expand data and open samples.csv. Confirm that the uploaded file opens in the remote editor.

For an edit, save with Cmd+S or Ctrl+S; that updates the remote file directly. No download-edit-upload cycle is needed. This small GUI transfer is suitable for the lecture’s scripts and tiny input. For a large dataset use the group’s recommended service, commonly Globus, and check transfer completion before starting analysis. Next open a new remote terminal in this same project folder.

title: Open a terminal in the same project
body:
VS Code → Terminal → New Terminal
hostname
cd /projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
pwd
hostnameCheck which computer is running the shell.
cdUse the same remote demo folder as Explorer.
pwdConfirm the current folder before running commands.

Run one line, press Enter, wait for the prompt, then continue.
notes:
The terminal is the text window; the shell reads commands. Open a new terminal inside the remote VS Code window. hostname identifies the remote computer; an illustrative result is cc-login1. It should identify a login host at this stage. cd sets the working directory to the uploaded project, and pwd prints that directory, for example /projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo after replacing the group placeholder. cd often prints nothing on success; that is normal. Replace the project path with the actual authorized one.

The prompt often shows the user, machine, and folder; its exact form varies. When a transcript includes a dollar sign before a command, do not type that sign. The shell is on a login node at this stage. Small file inspections are appropriate here; the analysis itself will be submitted to compute resources. Next learn how to read a command before adding options.

title: Read the program, options, and path in a command
body:
head -n 5 data/samples.csv
Programhead displays the beginning of a text file.
Option + value-n 5 asks for the first five lines.
File pathdata/samples.csv names the input.

Quotes keep a path together: head -n 5 "data/samples.csv". They are required for paths containing spaces.
notes:
Read the line left to right: run head, request five lines, and use this file. A shorter file produces fewer than five lines. The first word names the program; subsequent words are arguments. Options alter the program’s behavior. Not every option takes a separate value, and the same letter can mean something different in another program.

The shell uses spaces to separate arguments, so quotes keep a path with spaces together. The quoted path on this slide exists in the supplied demo. Its quotes are optional because this particular path contains no spaces; the command returns the same output either way. The colored parts are a reading aid, not text to type. This same reading habit will help with ls options and Slurm resource requests.

title: Navigate the uploaded project
body:
Transcript: type commands after $; other lines are output
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
$ cd data
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo/data
$ cd ..
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
$ cd ~
$ pwd
/u/YOUR_NETID
$ cd -
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
CommandMeaning
pwdPrint the current folder
cd dataEnter the data subfolder
cd ..Go up one folder
cd ~Go to your home folder
cd -Return to the previous folder

cd - also prints its destination. The next pwd confirms it.

. current folder · .. parent · /projects/… absolute path · data/… relative path
notes:
Follow the entire transcript in order. Start with pwd in demo. cd data enters the input subfolder, and the next pwd shows the full path ending in /demo/data. cd .. goes up to demo; pwd confirms that the last /data component has disappeared. cd ~ goes to the user’s home folder, shown as /u/YOUR_NETID on ICC. pwd now confirms home instead of the project path.

Finally cd - returns to the previous directory, which in this sequence is demo. Unlike the other successful cd commands shown here, cd - prints the destination itself. Its path therefore appears once immediately after cd -, and again after the explicit pwd check. The repeated path is expected. The final working folder is demo, ready for the next slide. Replace the project and NetID placeholders with the approved values.

The highlighted dollar-prefixed lines are commands; type only what follows the dollar sign. Other lines are illustrative output. An absolute path starts with a slash. A relative path starts from the current folder. Dot means the current folder, double dot the parent, and tilde home. cd - means previous directory, not necessarily the parent. Names are case-sensitive. Next list the input folder’s contents without moving out of demo.

title: List files and inspect their details
body:
CommandWhat changes
lsList visible names
ls -aInclude dot-prefixed entries
ls -lShow details such as size and date
ls -lhUse readable sizes, such as K or M
ls -lahCombine all three options
Illustrative listing lines; total lines omitted
$ ls data
samples.csv
$ ls -a data
.  ..  samples.csv
$ ls -l data
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group 58 Oct 27 10:00 samples.csv
$ ls -lh data
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group 58 Oct 27 10:00 samples.csv
$ ls -lah data
drwxr-xr-x 2 user group 4.0K Oct 27 10:00 .
drwxr-xr-x 3 user group 4.0K Oct 27 10:00 ..
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group   58 Oct 27 10:00 samples.csv

The CSV is only 58 bytes, so -h still shows 58. Later, ls -a will reveal the .venv folder we create.
notes:
Remain in demo after the previous slide. Every command on the right lists the same data subfolder; ls does not change the current directory. Compare each command with its matching definition on the left. Plain ls shows samples.csv. ls -a adds the dot entry for data itself and the double-dot entry for its parent, demo. Hidden names begin with a dot. The project’s .venv does not exist yet; after setup, ls -a in demo will show it.

ls -l adds details. Read one file line from left to right: permissions, link count, owner, group, size, modification date/time, and filename. The owner, group, timestamps, directory sizes, and link counts shown here are illustrative, so the viewer should not expect identical metadata. For readability the separate total lines printed by long directory listings are omitted. The permissions are shown so the output looks recognizable; a detailed permission lesson is outside this introduction.

The supplied samples.csv is exactly 58 bytes. Therefore ls -lh still displays 58 for this small file; -h does not force every size into kilobytes. Larger values use units such as K or M. ls -lah combines long, all, and human-readable: it includes both dot entries and the file details. The illustrated 4.0K directory entries are filesystem-dependent and do not represent the total size of their contents; du -sh measures folder disk usage later. We have confirmed the input is present. Next create a place for outputs.

title: Creating, copying, moving, and deleting
body:
CommandResult
mkdir resultsCreate one new folder
mkdir -p results/qcCreate missing parent folders; allow existing folders
cp -i notes.txt notes_backup.txtCopy a file; ask before overwriting
cp -r data data_backupCopy a folder and its contents to a new folder
mv -i notes_backup.txt notes_old.txtRename or move; ask before overwriting
rm -i notes_old.txtAsk before deleting this file

cp and mv: source first, destination second. Shell deletion normally has no Trash recovery.
notes:
These operations are also available in VS Code Explorer. Continue in the uploaded demo folder. The directory should not already contain results in a fresh copy. mkdir results creates a folder; if it already exists, that command reports an error. mkdir -p results/qc creates missing parents and accepts directories that already exist. No output often means the command succeeded; use ls to inspect the result.

cp creates another copy; mv changes a name or location. The -i option asks before overwriting an existing destination. cp -r includes subfolders; the shown destination data_backup should not already exist. Demonstrate only with the tiny supplied data, since copying real raw data may consume a large quota. rm -i asks before removal. Identify the exact file before answering. Do not demonstrate recursive deletion or removal with wildcards. If a workflow mentions touch, explain that touch run-notes.txt creates an empty file if absent, or updates timestamps if it exists; it does not open an editor.

title: Inspecting a small text file
body:
CommandUse
cat notes.txtPrint the entire small file
head -n 5 data/samples.csvRead the header and first rows
less notes.txtBrowse text; press q to leave
Output of head for the included sample table
sample_id,reads
sample_A,1000
sample_B,1500
sample_C,1200

Preview a few rows before running the analysis. Avoid printing a huge file with cat.
notes:
cat is convenient for a short configuration or note. head shows a bounded number of lines and is a better first look at a large text table. The included CSV contains four lines, so head -n 5 prints all four. Identify the header, comma delimiter, sample names, and values. These are toy values, not research results.

less allows scrolling without printing the whole file at once; q returns to the shell. An image, R object, HDF5 file, or compressed file is not ordinary text. Use a suitable viewer or tool. VS Code can open the same small text files through Explorer. This command version is useful in instructions and when the editor is unavailable.

title: Find a file, then find text inside it
body:
Search filenames within data and its subfolders
find data -type f -name "*.csv"
-type fMatch files; -name tests their names against the quoted pattern.
"*.csv"The * matches any text before .csv.
Search inside this file; -n includes line numbers
grep -n "sample_B" data/samples.csv
Expected grep output: line 3 contains the match
3:sample_B,1500
notes:
find searches file names in a directory tree. data is the starting folder, -type f selects files, and -name applies a filename pattern. Keep *.csv quoted here so find receives the pattern instead of the shell expanding it first. The expected find output is data/samples.csv. Limit the search to the relevant project folder.

grep searches the text inside a named file. -n adds the line number, so the output 3:sample_B,1500 means the match occurs on line three. Neither command modifies the input. Next count the lines and check disk usage to confirm the small input’s size.

title: Count lines and check disk usage
body:
Run this command
wc -l data/samples.csv
Expected output; do not type this line
4 data/samples.csv
wc -lCount lines in this text file.
4 linesOne header plus three sample rows.
Check space used by the input folder
du -sh data

-s gives one summary total · -h uses readable units such as K or M

Line count is not automatically sample count. Disk usage is not your remaining quota.
notes:
Run wc -l first. The shown output is four because the supplied CSV ends each of its four lines with a newline. Explain one header plus three samples. Real files may have extra headers, comments, or multiline records, so the interpretation depends on the format.

du reports disk usage. -s summarizes the folder into one total, and -h chooses human-readable units. du -sh combines those two options. The exact disk-usage value varies with the filesystem, so we do not promise a particular value. The input is now located and checked. Next see how to look up a command and use common terminal shortcuts.

title: Help and everyday terminal shortcuts
body:
Command / keyUse when needed
man lsOpen the manual; press q to leave
head --helpShow the Linux command’s built-in help
TabComplete a file or folder name
↑ / historyRecall previous commands / list shell history
Ctrl+CInterrupt the current foreground command
clear / exitClear the display / leave the current shell

Keep this shell open for the next step. Use exit only when you intend to leave it.
notes:
Options are command-specific; check the manual or built-in help when uncertain. Not every program supports --help, and a Mac’s built-in utility may differ from the Linux version on ICC. The examples in the lecture target the remote Linux shell. Tab completion reduces typing and capitalization errors; the up arrow retrieves an earlier command for inspection and editing.

history lists previously entered commands; it can include sensitive arguments, so do not put passwords or tokens in commands. Ctrl+C affects the command currently running in the foreground. clear only clears the visible terminal display, not files or job logs. exit leaves the current shell: it can end an interactive allocation or disconnect SSH depending on where you are. Use hostname and pwd whenever the context is uncertain. The next section turns these commands into a scheduled job.

title: Slurm runs work on allocated resources
body:
LOGIN NODE
Prepare and submithello.sbatchYour terminal stays here.
sbatch→
SlurmWait for resourcesThe scheduler
Allocate→
COMPUTE NODE
Run the jobhello.sbatchThe program runs here.
↕↕
Same shared demo/ folderInput · scripts · output

Batch: submit a script. Interactive: request a compute shell with srun.

Submit on the login node; the job runs on an allocated compute node.
notes:
Follow the upper arrows as a logical sequence, not a literal network diagram. On the login node, edit and save hello.sbatch, then submit it with sbatch. Slurm is scheduling software: it can hold the request pending until suitable resources are available. Once allocated, a compute node runs the job. Slurm is not an intermediate computer where the project files must be copied.

Point to the two vertical connections and the single shared demo folder. Both nodes can reach that same approved project location. Slurm runs the submitted script; the job reads inputs and writes output there. We do not copy the whole project to another computer for every submission.

Submitting a batch job leaves the current terminal on the login node. The batch job can continue after the laptop disconnects. An interactive job, introduced later with srun, instead starts a shell on an allocated compute node. It does not automatically move all VS Code execution features to that node. Both routes need allocated resources. Next inspect the tiny hello.sbatch file before submitting it.

title: Read a Slurm batch script line by line
body:
Select a line

Choose your assigned allocation.

01Use Bash to read the commands.
02Give the job a recognizable name.
03Choose your assigned allocation.
04Choose an eligible queue.
05Request one compute node.
06Request one task for this program.
07Reserve one CPU for that task.
08Request 1 GiB of RAM per node.
09Set a five-minute running-time limit.
10Print a message into the job output.

Edit these lines inside hello.sbatch in VS Code, then save. Submit it from the terminal after reviewing the resource settings.
notes:
Open hello.sbatch in the remote editor. Lines beginning with #SBATCH are requests to Slurm. They must appear before the executable commands. The echo command prints one message. The first line, #!/bin/bash, selects Bash to interpret the file. Bash is the shell program. #SBATCH is a special marker read by Slurm, while ordinary lines beginning with # are comments to Bash. The .sbatch name is a useful convention; this is still a plain text file. Do not paste the file contents into a live terminal. Click each line to see its meaning.

Use this tiny job to establish the mechanism before adding analysis software. Slurm reads the directives only when submitted through sbatch. Running bash hello.sbatch would execute echo on the current machine and ignore the resource requests as comments. The five-minute setting is the job’s maximum runtime, not a lecture timing label.

title: Set nodes, tasks, CPUs, memory, and time for a job
body:
Example resource request: count the node, the tasks, then the CPUs.

--nodes=11 computer
--ntasks=22 tasks in the whole job
--cpus-per-task=22 CPUs reserved for each task
Node 1One computer
Task 1One program process
CPUCPU
Task 2One program process
CPUCPU
2 tasks × 2 CPUs/task = 4 CPUs requestedntasks is already the total; do not multiply by nodes again.

Reserving resources does not launch the tasks or make the program parallel.

Keep hello.sbatch at: 1 node · 1 task · 1 CPU/task
--mem=1G1 GiB of RAM per node--time=00:05:00Runtime limit: hours:minutes:seconds
notes:
Use the diagram as a counting example, not a replacement for the preceding hello.sbatch file. First trace the outer border: one node is one computer, so --nodes=1. Then count the two task boxes: --ntasks=2 requests resources for two tasks across the whole job. A task is a program process in this example, not a sample, a file, or a line in the script. Finally count the two CPU blocks inside each task: --cpus-per-task=2 reserves two CPUs for each process.

There are four requested CPUs: two total tasks times two CPUs per task. Do not multiply by the node count again; --ntasks is already the total across the allocation, not a per-node number. The drawing shows requested resources, not all hardware in the computer or a promise that the whole node is reserved exclusively. Slurm may allocate additional resources depending on site policy and allocation granularity. A Slurm CPU can represent a physical core or a hardware thread depending on cluster configuration, so the blocks are labeled CPUs.

sbatch submits the script and requests resources; it does not automatically start the specified number of program processes. A plain python analysis.py command still starts one process. Launching multiple tasks needs the appropriate launcher and software support; a multithreaded program must also be configured to use the CPUs assigned to its task. We are explaining resource counts here, not adding a parallel-programming step to the lecture.

Return to the actual hello.sbatch values in the bottom strip: one node, one task, and one CPU per task. Keep those settings for the next submission. --mem=1G requests one GiB of RAM per node, not disk storage. --time=00:05:00 uses hours:minutes:seconds and limits runtime after the job starts, excluding queue waiting. These are tiny demonstration settings, not estimates for every dataset. Next submit the saved hello job.

title: Submit the first job: hello.sbatch
body:
In the remote demo folder, after saving the file
pwd
ls hello.sbatch
sbatch hello.sbatch
Illustrative response: record this job ID
Submitted batch job 123456

This first job prints a message. It does not run analysis.py yet.
notes:
Replace the account and partition placeholders in hello.sbatch with the approved pair, then save the remote file. pwd should identify demo and ls should find the job file. sbatch sends that file to Slurm. The example response uses job ID 123456; a live submission returns its own ID.

The job may wait before running. Saving a file is not submission, and the editor’s Run button is not sbatch. A batch job can continue after the laptop disconnects because the scheduler owns it. Next inspect its queue state, then open the message it produced.

title: Checking the queue and stopping a job
body:
-u selects your user; run squeue again to refresh the snapshot
squeue -u YOUR_NETID
StateMeaning
PDPending: waiting for resources or another scheduling condition
RRunning: the allocation has started
Only for an unwanted job; let hello finish in this example
scancel 123456

After hello leaves the queue: cat slurm-123456.out → My first HPC job. Use your job ID.
notes:
squeue shows queued and running work. The -u option filters the list to the supplied NetID. It produces one snapshot, not a continuously refreshing screen. Run it again when you want an updated view. A small job can finish before the command is entered. Pending is a scheduling state, not automatically an error. The queue listing can also show a reason. Avoid cancelling and resubmitting repeatedly without understanding that reason.

scancel stops the specified job. It is shown here as an option for an unwanted or incorrect submission, not as the next command to execute. Let hello finish, then run cat slurm-123456.out with the actual returned job ID. The default output file is in the submission folder and should contain My first HPC job. Disappearing from the queue alone does not prove success; inspect the log if the message is missing or an error appears. Ctrl+C in a log viewer does not cancel a batch job. The next slide explains output filenames and email settings for the analysis job.

title: Output files and email notifications
body:
In analysis.sbatch, before executable commands
#SBATCH --output=analysis-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=analysis-%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=YOUR_NETID@illinois.edu
SettingMeaning
--output / --errorFiles for ordinary output / diagnostic and error output
%jReplace with the job ID: analysis-123457.out
--mail-type=END,FAILAsk for notification at job end or failure
--mail-userThe recipient; use your address or remove both mail lines
notes:
These lines are already present in the supplied analysis.sbatch template. Explain them before that job is submitted; do not edit the completed hello job or duplicate the directives. --output and --error select filenames. Programs may send normal diagnostic messages to the error stream, so a nonempty .err file alone does not prove failure. %j is a Slurm filename token, not a shell variable.

END and FAIL are comma-separated event types. --mail-user gives the recipient address. Replace the placeholder or remove both mail directives. Email depends on site configuration, and an end notification is not proof that the output is scientifically correct. Plain filenames place the logs in the submission folder; if a log subfolder is used, create it before sbatch because Slurm opens the log before the script runs. Next are two optional resource choices for projects that need them; the tiny demo stays with its existing CPU settings.

title: When the analysis needs a GPU
body:
Optional GPU job: use a valid partition and configured GPU type
#SBATCH --partition=YOUR_GPU_PARTITION
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:GPU_TYPE:1
Inside an allocated NVIDIA GPU job
nvidia-smi
--gresRequest a generic resource; here gpu:TYPE:COUNT.
GPU_TYPE / final 1The configured GPU type / one GPU per allocated node.

The tiny demo needs no GPU. Add this only for software that supports and uses one.
notes:
A GPU allocation requires an eligible partition and account. ICC documents typed requests such as gpu:V100:1; that example is not a guarantee of availability in a particular allocation. Use the type and count your group can access. Requesting a GPU does not move an ordinary CPU-only program onto it.

nvidia-smi can confirm the NVIDIA GPU visible inside an allocated job. GPU device memory is different from the CPU RAM requested with --mem. Software may also need a compatible CUDA or framework installation; use its documented environment. Do not add a GPU just because the data are single-cell or spatial.

title: When a particular node is required
body:
Optional: use an actual eligible node name
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --nodelist=NODE_NAME
sinfo: inspect resources; -p selects the partition; -N lists nodes
sinfo -p YOUR_PARTITION -N
--nodes=1How many nodes you request
--nodelistWhich named node you request

Keep this out of the demo job. Name a node only for a specific need agreed with your group.
notes:
Node count and node identity are different. The first line requests one computer. The second line requests a named computer. Use a real node belonging to the authorized queue, not the literal placeholder or a login-node name. A visible node does not imply permission to use it.

A specific machine can be useful for a particular hardware requirement or a controlled comparison. It also reduces scheduling flexibility and can increase waiting. A GPU type or sufficient memory is often the underlying requirement, so ask whether that resource request is enough before pinning a node.

title: Open an interactive compute shell with srun
body:
From the login shell in demo: paste this whole block as one command
srun --account=YOUR_ACCOUNT --partition=YOUR_PARTITION \
  --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=2 \
  --mem=4G --time=00:15:00 --pty bash
srunStart a program on allocated compute resources.
--pty bashOpen an interactive terminal running the Bash shell.
After it startsRun hostname and pwd. Keep this shell open for Python setup.

A trailing \ continues a command onto the next line; nothing follows it on that line.
notes:
Use the valid account and partition saved during access setup. The resource options have the same meanings as those in the batch file. This setup request uses two CPUs, four GiB, and fifteen minutes as a small example. It is separate from the later one-CPU batch job. Adjust the request for the real installation’s needs.

Paste the displayed block as one command. The backslash must be the final character before the newline, with no trailing spaces. It tells the shell that the command continues. srun obtains an allocation if necessary and starts the requested program. --pty provides an interactive terminal, and bash names the shell program to run.

If a queued message appears, wait: the compute shell has not started yet. Once a prompt returns, run hostname; it should identify an allocated compute host. pwd should still be the shared demo path. If necessary, cd back to it. Keep this shell open for the next topic. Starting it does not move VS Code’s Run button or notebook kernel onto the compute node.

title: Make Python available in the compute shell
body:
Inside the allocation, in demo; use a version shown as available
module avail python
module load python/3.11.11
module list
CommandMeaning
module avail pythonList cluster modules matching Python
module load python/3.11.11Make this Python version available in this shell
module listConfirm which cluster modules are loaded

analysis.py imports pandas. Next, create a place to install that package.
notes:
A laptop installation is separate from a cluster installation. We are still in the allocated compute shell. module is the cluster’s software-selection command. avail searches available names, load changes the current shell’s software environment, and list confirms the selection. Read python/3.11.11 as a software name followed by its version. Verify availability and use the same compatible module in setup and the batch file.

Open analysis.py in VS Code and point to import pandas: that is the package this project needs. Loading Python alone does not install it. Next create an environment inside the remote demo folder. This cluster module command is different from Python’s -m option on the next slide.

title: Create a Python environment and install pandas
body:
Continue in the same compute shell and remote demo folder
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install pandas
ls -a
Create .venv-m runs Python’s venv utility; .venv is the new folder.
Activatesource applies the activation script to this current shell.
Install pandas-m pip runs pip with this Python; install names the action.

Wait for pip to finish and the prompt to return. Then check the import on the next slide.
notes:
Run these commands in order. Python’s -m runs a Python module as a command; it is unrelated to the cluster module command. venv creates a project environment, and the final .venv argument names its destination directory. source applies the activation script in the current shell so subsequent python commands use that environment. pip is Python’s package installer; install is its action, and pandas is the package to install.

The prompt may acquire a (.venv) prefix, but the import check is more useful than relying on the prompt’s appearance. Wait for the installer to finish before proceeding; a download in progress is not completion. ls -a now reveals .venv. The files live in the remote shared project folder. Activation affects only this shell, so a new terminal or job must activate again. Do not upload a laptop virtual environment. Next verify the installed package before leaving this allocation.

title: Check that pandas imports and save package versions
body:
-c executes the quoted Python code immediately
python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"
import pandasCheck that this Python can load the package.
Print versionprint(pandas.__version__) displays the installed version; expect a version number.
freeze lists installed package versions; > writes them into this file
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt

Continue only after the import succeeds. Keep this shell open for the next slide.
notes:
The environment remains active from the preceding slide; do not open a new terminal between setup and this check. Python -c runs the code inside quotes. The semicolon separates two Python statements: import the package, then print its version. __version__ is the package’s version attribute. The exact version depends on the installation, so no fixed version number is promised.

If an import error appears, stop and fix the selected module, environment, or installation before submitting. A successful download does not establish a working import. pip freeze lists the installed distributions and versions. The shell’s greater-than operator writes that output into requirements.txt, replacing an existing file. This records the environment; it does not reinstall anything. Next explain what remains when the current shell ends.

title: The environment stays; activation is per shell
body:
Install packagespython -m pip install pandasAfter creating and activating .venv
Write files→
Shared project storage
demo/.venv/Python + installed packagesThese files remain.
Activate in each new shell or jobsource .venv/bin/activate
Current compute shell
python→.venv/bin/python
Same existing.venvNo reinstall
A later batch job
python→.venv/bin/python

After setup, exit leaves the compute shell; the .venv files remain.
notes:
Start at the upper arrow. In the previous steps we created .venv and activated it before installing pandas. The pip command writes package files into that selected environment. The folder lives in shared project storage and persists when the interactive compute allocation ends. This diagram summarizes the distinction; it is not a new command sequence to repeat now.

Now trace the lower two examples. source .venv/bin/activate adjusts the current shell so its python command selects .venv/bin/python. It neither downloads the packages again nor starts a compute allocation. A later batch job selects the same existing environment by repeating the activation command. The two boxes depict separate shells, not a transfer of activation from one shell to the other. In both cases load the compatible Python module first, as already demonstrated. A child process inherits its parent shell environment, but a separately started terminal or job should not be assumed to have this setup.

Finally, importing is a third action inside the running program: import pandas loads installed package code so the calculation can use it. For R, library loads a package after its library location is configured. requirements.txt records Python package versions; R sessionInfo() records R session details. These records do not capture every system dependency. When setup is complete, type exit once to leave the interactive compute shell and release its allocation. Run hostname and pwd to confirm the original login host and project folder; if the allocation has already ended, check the host before typing exit. The original login shell does not inherit activation from the ended compute shell. The next slide is an optional Conda route using a separate allocated setup session, not another step for the prepared Python environment.

title: Create a Conda environment from a supplied file
body:
Alternative route when the project supplies environment.yml
module avail miniconda3
module load YOUR_CONDA_MODULE
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda run -n analysis python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"
environment.ymlRecords the environment name and requested packages
-f environment.ymlRead the environment specification from this file.
-n analysisUse the environment named analysis (from name: analysis in the file).

Use a separate allocated setup session. Expect a pandas version; this replaces the .venv route.
notes:
Use this route when the project already provides a Conda environment file. The teaching environment.yml is in the separate examples directory, not the minimal demo folder. Upload it to the remote project only if using this alternative. Replace the module placeholder with a name available on ICC. The -f option names the input YAML file. Its name: analysis line gives the environment name, which -n selects in conda run. The final Python command checks the import and prints the version; no version means the check has not succeeded. Exit the allocated shell when this alternative setup is complete. conda run avoids requiring an interactive activation setup in the batch shell.

This is an alternative to the venv route, not an instruction to nest both. Follow the project’s supported package channels and versions. Check where Conda stores environments and caches so they fit the quota; project storage may be preferable. The included YAML is a small teaching example, not a pinned environment for a scientific pipeline.

title: Prepare a Python batch job with its environment
body:
1 · Beginning of analysis.sbatch
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=analysis
#SBATCH --account=YOUR_ACCOUNT
#SBATCH --partition=YOUR_PARTITION
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=1G
#SBATCH --time=00:05:00
2 · Continue in the same file, after the left column
#SBATCH --output=analysis-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=analysis-%j.err

set -e
module load python/3.11.11
source .venv/bin/activate
python analysis.py

set -e stops this script if setup fails. Replace placeholders and save the file before submitting.
notes:
Read the two columns as one file: the left column first, followed by the right column. All #SBATCH directives precede executable commands. This is the same one-node, one-task, one-CPU, one-GiB tiny demonstration as the supplied file. Larger research workflows need their own resource estimates. The output and error directives select the two log filenames; Slurm replaces %j with the job ID. These plain filenames put logs in the submission folder. The supplied template also contains optional email directives: --mail-type=END,FAIL requests messages when the job ends or fails, and --mail-user sets the recipient. Replace the address or remove both mail lines.

The lower part repeats the module and activation that passed the import check. set -e stops the shell script if setup fails. python analysis.py reads the same data/samples.csv and will write results/summary.csv. Package installation is not repeated. Save the file in VS Code. The next slide submits this analysis job, which is different from the earlier hello job.

title: Submit the analysis job
body:
In the login shell, from the demo folder
pwd
ls data/samples.csv analysis.py analysis.sbatch
sbatch analysis.sbatch
Illustrative analysis job ID; hello used 123456
Submitted batch job 123457
Check whether this new job is pending or running
squeue -u YOUR_NETID

Use this new job ID for the analysis logs and completion checks.
notes:
The project is now ready: input, script, job file, and package environment are in place. Confirm the working directory and filenames. Submit the saved analysis.sbatch. The illustrative new ID is 123457, deliberately different from the earlier hello job. In a real session, always use the returned ID.

The scheduler may report PD while waiting and R once it runs. The configured log filenames become analysis-123457.out and analysis-123457.err. They may not exist until the job begins. Wait for the job to start before trying to read them. Next follow the job log, then open the generated output in VS Code.

title: Watch job output and search the error log
body:
After the analysis job starts and the log exists
tail -n 20 analysis-123457.out
tail -f analysis-123457.out
First press Ctrl+C to stop tail; then search the error log
grep -in "error" analysis-123457.err
Ctrl+CStop tail; the submitted job keeps running.
Need to cancel?scancel 123457 cancels this analysis job.

tail: -n 20 = last 20 lines, -f = follow new output · grep: -i = ignore case, -n = line numbers
notes:
Use the analysis job’s ID, not the earlier hello ID. tail -n 20 reads the last twenty lines and returns. tail -f initially reads the last ten lines and then follows new output. Ctrl+C stops this foreground viewer; it does not cancel the submitted batch job. scancel would cancel the specified job.

While tail -f is running, the shell is not ready for another command. Press Ctrl+C, wait for the prompt, and only then run grep. The -n 20 option of tail selects the last twenty lines, while -f keeps following new output. grep -in searches error text case-insensitively and adds line numbers. A match is a clue to inspect, and no match is not proof of success. Some messages are buffered or sent to a different stream. Both logs can also be opened in VS Code. Next open the output in VS Code. Inspect the logs and the actual output contents; leaving the queue or finding no error text alone does not establish success.

title: Open the result in VS Code
body:
Explorer → resultsOpen your output file, such as summary.csv, and inspect its contents.
Keep it remoteRead or edit the file without downloading it first.
Need a local copy?Right-click summary.csv and choose Download…
Other output typesViewer
Logs / PNG / JPEGBuilt-in text or image viewer
CSV / TSVText editor; Rainbow CSV adds column colors
PDF / notebooksA PDF viewer extension / Microsoft Jupyter viewer
notes:
Return to the same Explorer folder used to upload the project. Refresh Explorer if necessary, expand results, and open summary.csv. Check that the output exists, is readable, and contains the result expected for your input; an empty or incomplete file needs investigation. Download only when a local copy is useful; reading a remote result does not require copying it back first.

Real analyses may also produce plots, reports, tables, and notebooks. Use the appropriate viewer extension and follow VS Code’s local-versus-SSH installation prompt. A viewer does not allocate compute resources; opening a notebook is different from running cells. We have now completed the example. The remaining slides transfer the routine to other projects and cover troubleshooting.

title: Run an R script as a Slurm batch job
body:
R commands below the #SBATCH resource settings
module load R
Rscript analysis.R
After copying and configuring the R templates from examples/
sbatch analysis_R.sbatch
Same inputdata/samples.csv
R outputresults/summary_R.csv

This example uses base R; no additional package installation is needed.
notes:
The main Python example is complete. For an R project, replace the program and software setup with the R route. The full examples directory contains analysis.R and analysis_R.sbatch; these are not extra steps required by the minimal Python demo. Copy both into the intended remote project, configure the job, and submit from that folder.

module load R makes the cluster R interpreter available in the job; use a module name available on your cluster. Rscript runs an R file without opening the interactive R console. The supplied calculation uses base R and needs no add-on package or custom package library. Its output is summary_R.csv, not summary.csv. Repeat the same job-state, log, and result checks using the new returned ID. Real workflows need resource settings based on their own tools and inputs.

title: Common errors and the first useful check
body:
What you seeCheck first
No such file or directorypwd, the path, and the filename’s capitalization
Command not foundThe required module or environment
No module named… / no package called…The active Python or R library, then installation
OUT_OF_MEMORY / TIMEOUTRequested RAM or runtime and the tool’s actual needs
Invalid account / partitionThe allocation and queue pair assigned to you
Permission denied / quota exceededThe target folder’s access and available quota
notes:
Work from the specific error instead of resubmitting unchanged. A path error usually starts with the working directory and exact name. An import error starts with the selected interpreter or library. A resource failure needs the tool’s usage and a sensible revised request, not arbitrary large numbers.

Share the job number, job file, exact error, and software version with the lab contact or ICC support. Avoid sending large datasets or credentials as part of a help request. If the input is still uploading or the environment is incomplete, fix that before another job submission.
